blocks.text: A password on a Pages file has one clear job. It keeps people who receive the file from reading it without the password. That matters when a file leaves your Mac, whether you email a draft, put a contract on a shared drive or hand a template to a colleague. The protection travels with the file, so it still applies after the file is out of your hands.
What the password does and what it does not do

In Pages, a password encrypts the document. Apple's Mac guide says adding a password encrypts the file. Someone who has a copy but not the password cannot read the contents in Pages. The protection stays with the file, even if you copy it to a USB drive or upload it.

It does not protect the rest of your Mac. If someone can sign in to your Mac account, they can still reach your other files. The password guards one document, nothing more. Treat your Mac login as the first lock and the document password as the second.
Before you add a password

Start by saving the latest edits. Press ⌘S, then look at the document name in the window. If it shows changes you did not make, stop and check which copy is open. The password goes on the file that is open, so make sure that is the copy you mean.

Decide whether you need an unprotected copy. Many people protect a file they plan to send, then keep a working copy open. Duplicate the file with ⇧⌘S before you add a password. Keep the copy somewhere you can reach, because the password is only one way in.

Pick the password before you open the dialog. Apple's Mac guide says the password cannot be recovered if you forget it. Choose one you can remember, or save it in a password manager first. A sticky note on the monitor defeats the point, so keep the password somewhere private.
Set a password in Pages on Mac

The Set Password dialog stays short, but one checkbox changes depending on your setup. If Touch ID is not set up, you see Remember this password in my keychain. If Touch ID is set up, you see Open with Touch ID instead. Apple's guide describes both options.

The keychain option saves the password on this Mac, so Pages can fill it in when you open the file. The Touch ID option lets you open the file with your fingerprint. Both save typing. The keychain entry lives on this Mac, so think about who else uses it before you choose that option.
Check that the password works

Close the document and open it again. Pages should ask for the password before it shows any content. If the file opens with no prompt, you probably have the unprotected copy open. Check the file name first, because the duplicate and the original can look almost the same.
Try a wrong password once. The file should refuse it. This takes a few seconds, and it catches a typo before you depend on the file for a deadline.
Change or remove a Pages password

Open the protected document and enter the existing password. Choose File > Change Password. Apple's guide says you enter the requested information and click Change Password. To remove protection, type the old password and click Remove Password instead.
The table below lists each password task with its menu path and what you type. Keep it handy if you manage several files, because the steps differ slightly for removal.

rows: A new password, then Set Password
The old password, then a new one and Change Password
The old password, then Remove Password
System Settings > Touch ID & Password, then Pages > Settings
A fingerprint, then Use Touch ID
Nothing. This is not password protection.

blocks.text: Set up Touch ID for Pages documents

Touch ID needs a fingerprint in macOS first. Open System Settings, go to Touch ID & Password, and choose Add Fingerprint. Then open Pages, choose Pages > Settings, and select Use Touch ID. Only documents set up with Open with Touch ID use it.
Touch ID is a convenience. It does not replace the password on the document. You still set one with File > Set Password first, and Touch ID then opens the file you already protected.
Protect a shared Pages document
Shared files need more care. Anyone with editing permission can add, change or delete the password on a shared document. A password only holds if the people with editing access are people you trust.

A document can have only one password. A new or changed password applies to that version and later versions. If a shared copy has no password, or an older one, stop sharing, add a unique password, then share again.
Password in Pages for iCloud uses the More button

In Pages for iCloud, you do not use the File menu. Click the More button in the toolbar and choose Set Password. Enter a password and a password hint, then click Set Password. A secure symbol appears on the thumbnail in the document manager.

Changing the password works the same way. Under More, choose Change Password. Enter the old password, then type a new one or choose Remove Password. Pages for iCloud accepts numerals, upper- and lowercase letters and special characters.
If you forget a Pages password

Apple says a forgotten password cannot be recovered. Its iCloud guide says the same thing. Your options are narrow, so check them in order. First, see whether you saved the password in your keychain. Open the Keychain Access app and search for the document name.

If nothing turns up, the file stays closed. Your best next move is an unprotected copy from a backup, a duplicate you made earlier, or a version someone else sent you. Keep copies going forward, so one lost password does not cost you the work.
Locking is not the same as a password

Pages has a separate option that people mix up with password protection. The Locked checkbox sits in the document name popup. It stops accidental edits. It does not stop anyone from opening the file, and anyone can turn the lock off. Use it to guard a finished draft from yourself, and use a password when someone else must not read the file.
Common mistakes when protecting a Pages file

items: Protecting the only copy. Duplicate the file first, then protect the copy you plan to send.
Saving the password nowhere. Apple says a forgotten password cannot be recovered, so store it before you click Set Password.
Trusting Locked as security. Anyone can turn the lock off.
Assuming collaborators cannot change the password. Anyone with editing permission can change it on a shared document.
Opening the wrong copy and assuming it is protected. Check the file name in the window before you close it.
Relying on a keychain entry on a shared Mac. Anyone who uses that Mac account may be able to reach it.

blocks.text: Which Pages version these steps cover

Pages on Mac now comes in two lines. MacRumors reports that Pages 15.1 arrived on January 28, 2026, as a new, separate Apple Creator Studio edition. The older Mac app was updated to 14.5 only to say it no longer gets new features.

Apple's Mac password guide does not name a version, so check your own File menu. If Set Password is missing, check which Pages you opened, because the older app and the 15.1 edition are separate apps. Reports also differ on the macOS requirement for Pages 15.1, so check the App Store listing before you update.
Next steps after you protect a document

Once the file is protected, the next task is usually layout. If your document is long, the [table of contents guide](/how-to/create-a-table-of-contents-in-pages) walks through building one in Pages on Mac.

If you write for a living, the [Pages for writers on Mac](/for/writers/pages) page lists templates, drafts and layout tips. For footnotes that restart by chapter, see [the footnote numbering guide](/for/writers/problems/pages-footnote-numbering-restart-sections).

faq.question: Does a password on a Pages document encrypt it?
faq.answer: Yes. Apple's Mac guide says adding a password encrypts the file. Without the password, Pages cannot show the contents, so keep the password where you can reach it.

faq.question: Can I recover a forgotten Pages password?
faq.answer: Usually not. Apple says the password cannot be recovered if you forget it. The exception is a keychain entry on the same Mac, if you chose to save the password there.

faq.question: Can I password protect a document in Pages for iCloud?
faq.answer: Yes. Click the More button in the toolbar, choose Set Password, enter a password and a password hint, then click Set Password.

faq.question: Does the password stop collaborators from editing?
faq.answer: Not in the way you might expect. Anyone with editing permission can add, change or delete the password on a shared document, so share a protected file only with people you trust.

faq.question: Is locking a document the same as a password?
faq.answer: No. A locked document prevents accidental edits, and anyone can turn the lock off. Use Set Password when the file must stay closed to other people.

faq.question: Do I need a subscription to use Pages?
faq.answer: No. MacRumors reports that Pages stays free to download and use. Apple Creator Studio, which includes Pages, costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year in the U.S. TidBITS lists $129.99 per year, so check the current price before you pay.

faq.question: Can a document have more than one password?
faq.answer: No. A document can have only one password, and a new or changed password applies to that version and later versions.

faq.question: Which Pages version do these steps match?
faq.answer: Apple's Mac guide does not name a version. Pages 15.1 is the newer Creator Studio edition, released January 28, 2026 according to MacRumors, and the older Mac app stays at 14.5 with no new features.

task: Password protect a Pages document on Mac
appliesTo: Pages on Mac, including the 15.1 Creator Studio edition and the older app
requirements: Pages on Mac. Apple's Mac guide describes these steps without naming a version.
The document open and active in Pages, so the File menu acts on it.
A password you can remember or store safely, since Apple says it cannot be recovered.
Touch ID is optional. Without it, the Set Password dialog shows a keychain checkbox instead.

steps.name: Save the document first
steps.text: Open the document in Pages and save your latest edits. Press ⌘S so the file matches what you see on screen before you protect it.
steps.tip: Saving first means the protected version holds your latest edits, not an older draft.

steps.name: Duplicate it if you need an open copy
steps.text: Choose File > Duplicate and keep the new copy unprotected, somewhere you can reach it. Protect only the file you plan to send or share.
steps.tip: Name the copies so you can tell them apart, such as Budget and Budget Protected.

steps.name: Open the Set Password dialog
steps.text: Choose File > Set Password from the menu bar. The dialog asks for the information Pages needs to set the password.
steps.tip: If the item is missing, read the troubleshooting list on this page before you try again.

steps.name: Type a password you can keep
steps.text: Enter the password you want. Apple's guide says it cannot be recovered if you forget it, so choose one you will remember or store it somewhere safe before you continue.
steps.tip: Apple's iCloud guide says passwords can include numerals, upper- and lowercase letters and special characters.

steps.name: Choose the keychain or Touch ID option
steps.text: Without Touch ID, turn on the Remember this password in my keychain checkbox if you want Pages to remember it on this Mac. With Touch ID set up, you see Open with Touch ID instead.
steps.tip: The keychain entry stays on this Mac, so think about who else uses the account.

steps.name: Click Set Password
steps.text: Click Set Password to finish. Adding the password encrypts the document, so the file is protected from this point on.
steps.tip: Do not close the dialog by accident before you click, or the password will not be set.

steps.name: Close and reopen to test
steps.text: Close the document, then open it again from the same location. Pages should ask for the password before it shows any contents.
steps.tip: Try a wrong password once. It should not open, and then you can enter the right one.

troubleshooting.problem: I can't find Set Password in the File menu.
troubleshooting.fix: Make sure a document is open and active in the Pages window. Then read the File menu on your own Mac, since Apple's guide does not name a version and menus can differ between Pages releases.

troubleshooting.problem: Pages opens the file without asking for a password.
troubleshooting.fix: You probably have the unprotected copy open. Close it, check the file name, then open the copy you protected. Duplicates can look almost identical.

troubleshooting.problem: The shared copy has no password, or an older one.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop sharing, add a unique password with File > Set Password, then share the document again. Apple says a new password applies to that version and later versions.

troubleshooting.problem: Pages keeps asking for the password every time.
troubleshooting.fix: Next time, turn on the Remember this password in my keychain checkbox when you set the password. The checkbox appears only when Touch ID is not set up.

troubleshooting.problem: Touch ID does not open the protected file.
troubleshooting.fix: Add a fingerprint in System Settings > Touch ID & Password, then choose Pages > Settings and select Use Touch ID. Touch ID works on documents set up with Open with Touch ID.

troubleshooting.problem: A locked document still opens for other people.
troubleshooting.fix: The Locked checkbox stops accidental edits only. Anyone can turn the lock off, so use File > Set Password when the file must stay closed.
